To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the p20 domain is a highly conserved domain, which is found in caspase homologue enzymes of all organisms, including prokaryotes, and that this domain has been adapted for various functions in different species.
the structural diversity of caspases and their homologues in eubacteria, yeast and plants is much larger than originally anticipated.

(i) orthocaspases have been found in all domains, from prokaryotes to eukaryotes; (ii) they are involved in various processes of cell death; (iii) they exhibit different substrate specificites compared to metazoan caspases; (iv) they are involved also in processes other than cell death.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural and functional diversity of the p20-domain containing proteases, which are present in all domains of living organisms.
the structural and functional characterization of caspase-like proteases in non-metazoa and the role of these enzymes in programmed cell death and cell differentiation.
the elucidation of the role of caspase-like proteins in non-metazoa and the understanding of how these proteins evolved to perform their functions in these organisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of caspase-like proteases is not restricted to cell death, but rather is involved in a wide range of cellular processes, including cell differentiation, cell proliferation and cell death.
caspase homologue proteins are not involved in programmed cell death in non-metazoa.
the role of non-metazoon caspase homologue is not yet fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
caspase homologue enzymes are involved in many different processes, including cell death, but their role in this process is not yet completely elucidated.

the p20 domain-containing proteases of non-metazoa, which were initially proposed to execute cell death, are involved in the regulation of cell death, but also in other cellular processes, such as cell differentiation and ageing.
caspase homologue enzymes are involved in the control of cell death, but also in other important processes in the cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that
caspase-like proteases, although sharing the same catalytic domain, exhibit different biochemical properties and are likely involved in different processes.
orthocaspase homologues are present in all domains of living organisms, and their role in cell death has been overrated.
caspase homologue enzymes have evolved into a family of structurally diverse proteins with different substrate specificities, and that their role in cell death may be limited.
